parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a detailed follow-up within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk, and promptly provide safety instructions and updates.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a detailed follow-up within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk, and promptly provide safety instructions and updates.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a detailed follow-up within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk, and promptly provide safety instructions and updates. Reports must include the model, incident date and location, known consequences, and any immediate mitigation. Suspected incidents must not be omitted while an investigation is pending.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and statistically adequate sample. A model exceeding the 5% failure-rate benchmark must submit a corrective-action plan and undergo retesting; regulators may restrict marketing or installation if the manufacturer fails to mitigate the risk or evidence indicates serious or imminent danger.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and statistically adequate sample. Before market entry and after material design changes, manufacturers must submit per-model protocols, sample sizes, failure rates, and results to regulators and provide the same per-model results to customers considering or owning that model in clear, accessible form. Results must identify the protocol and test date. A model exceeding the 5% failure-rate benchmark must submit a corrective-action plan and undergo retesting; regulators may restrict marketing or installation if the manufacturer fails to mitigate the risk or evidence indicates serious or imminent danger. Manufacturers must promptly provide customers relevant corrective actions and material updates.

parameters.quote: New units must support secure remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized access and clear customer instructions. Manufacturers must retrofit already-installed units to provide this capability within six years of the standard’s effective date, prioritizing units subject to safety alerts or elevated risk.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New units must support secure remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized access and clear customer instructions. Manufacturers must retrofit already-installed units to provide this capability within six years of the standard’s effective date, prioritizing units subject to safety alerts or elevated risk.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New units must support secure remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized access and clear customer instructions. Manufacturers must retrofit already-installed units to provide this capability within six years of the standard’s effective date, prioritizing units subject to safety alerts or elevated risk. Where a safe retrofit is not technically feasible, the manufacturer must notify the regulator and affected customers and provide an approved alternative mitigation.

parameters.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after the standard’s adoption. The suppression system must be suitable for the battery chemistry and installation environment, and manufacturers must provide maintenance and replacement instructions to customers.

parameters.quote: A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. Manufacturers must notify the regulator and affected customers promptly upon determining that the trigger is exceeded, provide a corrective-action and recall plan, and report completion progress.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. Manufacturers must notify the regulator and affected customers promptly upon determining that the trigger is exceeded, provide a corrective-action and recall plan, and report completion progress.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers clear safety notices for incidents, hazards, corrective actions, and safe-use instructions, and must promptly update affected customers when material information changes. For each model, the annual thermal-incident rate is the number of confirmed thermal incidents during the preceding 12 months divided by that model’s installed units, expressed per 100,000 units. Manufacturers must maintain auditable incident and installed-unit records and provide the calculation and supporting data to the regulator. A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. Manufacturers must notify the regulator and affected customers promptly upon determining that the trigger is exceeded, provide a corrective-action and recall plan, and report completion progress. Verification or investigation must not delay protective action where evidence indicates an imminent or serious risk. Regulators may require a recall or other protective action earlier when the evidence indicates such a risk.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Halcyon’s flagship Ember 8 had a 3.9% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test
ground_truth_claims.message_text: Relevant evidence for S2/S5: Halcyon’s flagship Ember 8 had a 3.9% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test, and its thermal-incident rate was 9.9 per 100,000 installed units last year. Halcyon’s company-wide rate was 8.1 per 100,000. These figures indicate the proposed 8-per-100,000 model trigger would apply to the Ember 8; any rule should specify consistent rate calculation, verification, and prompt protective action.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Northwind’s Hearth 10 had 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year
ground_truth_claims.message_text: For comparison on S5, Northwind’s Hearth 10 had 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year—below the discussed model-level 8-per-100,000 trigger. A consistent model-level calculation and verification process would help apply the trigger fairly.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Northwind’s Hearth 10 measured a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test
ground_truth_claims.message_text: For consistent application of S2, Northwind’s Hearth 10 measured a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test. This is above the discussed 5% benchmark, so the draft’s corrective-action and retesting pathway—rather than automatic market exclusion—would be consequential. Results should be assessed using the same regulator-approved protocol and adequate sample requirements across models.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Halcyon had four thermal incidents last year that were not reported to any regulator
ground_truth_claims.message_text: Additional reporting evidence: Halcyon had four thermal incidents last year that were not reported to any regulator. This supports requiring auditable incident records and periodic reconciliation of incident reports against customer complaints, service records, and other available sources.

judge_section_notes: The final rules are strong on reporting (24h/72h), testing (55°C, 5% benchmark, customer and regulator results, no public publication), remote shut-off (new units and 6-year retrofit), fire suppression (36 months), and recall (8/100k mandatory with prompt notice). All four red lines are respected, and the main compromises are the six-year retrofit, 36-month suppression, and corrective-action pathway for S2 rather than automatic market exclusion. S2 and S5 have no phase-in periods, and S5 lacks an explicit serious-injury recall clause.
